sections.content: You know hedging expressions such as *parece que*, *según parece* and *podría decirse que* from B2 Unit 21. In demographic reports, caution is essential because two numbers that move together do not prove that one caused the other: *correlación* is not *causalidad*. To avoid overstating a finding, writers pair hedged verbs (*los datos parecen indicar*, *la muestra apunta a*, *el censo refleja*) with limits on what can be concluded (*no permiten concluir que*, *conviene interpretar esta cifra con prudencia*). Notice mood: affirmative *parece que* and *todo apunta a que* take the indicative, whereas negated *no permiten concluir que* or *no significa que* take the subjunctive.

sections.title: Hedging vs overclaiming
rows: Los datos parecen indicar un descenso paulatino.
Las cifras no permiten concluir que esa sea la única causa.
Conviene interpretar estos resultados con prudencia.

items.spanish: El censo refleja una fuerte correlación, pero no demuestra causalidad.
items.english: The census reflects a strong correlation, but does not prove causation.

items.spanish: Los resultados apuntan a un cambio lento en la estructura familiar.
items.english: The results point to a slow change in family structure.

items.spanish: Estas cifras no permiten concluir que la emigración sea el único factor.
items.english: These figures do not allow us to conclude that emigration is the only factor.

items.english: It is advisable to read the variations of a small sample with caution.

sections.content: English speakers often use "indicate" or "suggest" followed by a blunt claim that treats correlation as proof. And watch the mood shift: *los datos indican que hay* (indicative), but *los datos no permiten concluir que haya* (subjunctive).
